subject: Is it ok to discard slow chains?

messages.author: c82e7d89d213881d
messages.subject: Is it ok to discard slow chains?
parts:
Hi -- I'm fitting a model with 10 parallel chains (each with 2,000 iterations). It typically takes a couple of hours for the first chain to finish, and then another 2-3 hours for all of them to complete. When I intermittently inspect the fitted parameters, R_hat and N_Eff on the first several chains to complete, everything looks great; but if I include the last 2-3 chains to finish, the results don't look good anymore (and the average number of leap frog steps goes way up, to about 1,000).

Is it reasonable to simply discard the slow chains? I suspect there is something wrong with them (poor mixing, bad initialization, etc.), but am worried that I'd be cherry picking results if I just base my final analysis on the "good" ones.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it ok to discard slow chains?
parts: > Is it reasonable to simply discard the slow chains?

No.
No no.
No no no no no.
> I suspect there is something wrong with them (poor mixing, bad initialization, etc.), but am worried that I'd be cherry picking results if I just base my final analysis on the "good" ones.

Yup!

The problem with MCMC is that it has to work from _any_ initial condition
(okay, almost any for the math pedants). What’s happening here is that
the “good” chains are exploring only well-behaved regions of the posterior
and missing the more pathological regions. So they’re not really good,
they’re just ignorant of the bad. The “bad” chains are actually you’re
friend here — they find the pathological regions and let you know that
your model has some problems.

As Andrew noted you can often fix these pathological regions by
better parameterizations and other tricks. Try looking at pairs()
or the trace plots to identify where the problems are arising.

messages.author: c82e7d89d213881d
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it ok to discard slow chains?
parts:
Ok, thanks for the advice. Any tips on how to re-parameterize the attached model (or other tricks to fix things)?

If I initialize the chains at any reasonable point, the pathologies seem to disappear. Is that an ok solution, or is it really just the same thing as discarding the slow chains (since they were presumably slow because of their "bad" starting values).

Without initialization, the slow chains have step size an order of magnitude smaller than the fast ones and consistently run into the tree depth limit; if I increase max depth, it takes prohibitively long for the chains to complete.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it ok to discard slow chains?
parts:
Thanks for letting us know that worked. It can be hard to
converge in difficult problems, even for Stan, because the
convergence and adaptaiton present the canonical chicken-and-egg
problem, where you need good adaptation to converge and vice-versa.

Andrew's been thinking about various kinds of cross-chain adaptation,
but we have be careful that we can figure out how to do it without
destroying desirable properties of the sampler (not that anything we
do in warmup will destroy the theoretical properties of the sampler,
it's just that they might fail practically speaking and make it hard
to diagnose convergence).

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it ok to discard slow chains?
parts:
Nooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooo!
Those analyses are incredibly biased because
they optimize on the wrong parameters (step
size and number of leapfrog step instead of
step size and integration time) and their artificial
bounds on the number of leapfrog steps is
waaaaaaaaaay too small.

Anyways, NUTS (or its generalization!) is the right 
answer to the optimal integration time (proof coming 
soon!) and we know how to globally optimize

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it ok to discard slow chains?
parts:
BDA3, Section 5.3, Page 110, equation (5.9):

p(alpha, beta) propto (alpha + beta)^(-5/2)

If I'm doing my algebra right, that means

p(alpha + beta) = Pareto(alpha + beta | 1.5)

alpha and beta are hyperprior parameters for a Beta
distribution over tumor risks in rats. You reasoned
that making the following uniform would make sense

alpha / (alpha + beta) and sqrt(alpha + beta)

The suggestion that I think people want to see in order to
think about informative priors, is similar to what you
do, namely to reparameterize beta for mu in (0, 1) and phi > 0 as

Beta_mean(y | mu, phi) = Beta(y | mu * phi, (1 - mu) * phi)

I suggested in the manual

mu ~ uniform(0, 1);

and

phi ~ Pareto(1.5)

in attempt to follow section 5.3 of BDA.

We could put informative priors on both mu and phi. A beta's
a natural choice for mu, though you also consider logit transforming
it, and then we could use anything. We could also log-transform
phi to an unconstrained space.

In fact, the more I think about Stan computation, the more sense
it makes to start reparameterizing everything on the unconstrained
scale so we don't have to transform and pay the Jacobian cost in
autodiff. For example, the most natural seeming parameterization for
Beta would be this

Beta_unc(y | logit_mu, log_phi)

= Beta_mean(y | inv_logit(logit_mu), exp(log_phi)

= Beta(y | inv_logit(logit_mu) * exp(log_phi),
(1 - inv_logit(logit_mu)) * exp(log_phi))

but we could also just log transform the usual parameterization

Beta_unc_2(y | log_alpha, log_beta)

= Beta(y | exp(log_alpha), exp(log_beta))

- Bob
